Leaching dissolves the wanted component of an ore in a selective reagent. Tin ore, cassiterite \(SnO_2\), is amphoteric and dissolves in hot concentrated alkali as a stannate:

\(SnO_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SnO_3 + H_2O\)

The tin is later recovered from the soluble stannate, so alkali leaching is the concentration step for \(Sn\).

Copper and lead ores are sulphides concentrated by froth flotation, not alkali leaching; gold is leached with dilute \(NaCN\) in the presence of air (cyanide leaching), which is complexation, not alkali dissolution of an amphoteric oxide.

Answer: \(Sn\), option B.

The Freundlich isotherm is \(\frac{x}{m}=k\,p^{1/n}\) with \(n>1\), and its logarithmic form is \(\log\frac{x}{m}=\log k+\frac{1}{n}\log p\).

Graph A: \(\frac{x}{m}\) against \(p\) rises steeply and then flattens — the characteristic Freundlich curve, so it qualifies.

Graph B: \(\log\frac{x}{m}\) against \(\log p\) is a straight line of slope \(1/n\) and intercept \(\log k\) (marked 'constant'), which is exactly the logarithmic Freundlich form, so it qualifies.

Graph C: \(\frac{x}{m}\) against concentration \(c\) drawn as a straight line with a non-zero intercept. Freundlich in solution is \(\frac{x}{m}=k\,c^{1/n}\), a curve through the origin, not a line with an intercept, so C does not qualify.

Graph D: \(\frac{x}{m}\) against \(p^{1/n}\) is a straight line through the origin of slope \(k\), directly from the isotherm, so it qualifies.

A, B and D only, option B.

Split the overall reaction into half reactions.

Oxidation (anode): \(\frac{1}{2}H_2(g) \rightarrow H^+(aq) + e^-\), which needs a hydrogen electrode, \(Pt\,|\,H_2(g)\,|\,H^+\).

Reduction (cathode): \(AgCl(s) + e^- \rightarrow Ag(s) + Cl^-(aq)\), which is the silver–silver chloride electrode, \(AgCl(s)\,|\,Ag\).

Both \(H^+\) and \(Cl^-\) appear in the same solution, so the single electrolyte must supply both ions, i.e. \(HCl\). The cell is therefore

\(Pt\,|\,H_2(g)\,|\,HCl(aq)\,|\,AgCl(s)\,|\,Ag\)

which is option B.

Option A uses \(KCl\) and so cannot generate the \(H^+\) that appears in the reaction; option C has silver–silver chloride electrodes on both sides and no hydrogen electrode; option D uses \(AgNO_3\), which would make \(Ag^+ + e^- \rightarrow Ag\) the cathode reaction, not the reduction of \(AgCl\).

Portland cement without an additive sets within minutes because tricalcium aluminate hydrates almost instantly, which leaves no time to place the concrete. Gypsum, \(CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O\), is ground in at about \(2\text{–}3\%\); it reacts with the aluminate to form a thin coating of ettringite that blocks further rapid hydration. It does not promote hydration, does not accelerate setting, and does not itself supply hardness — the hardness comes from the calcium silicate hydrate gel.
